noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand the role of neurotransmitters at synapses

primer.text: You already know neurones carry electrical impulses at high speed. This note covers the one place that story has a gap — literally: neurones never touch, and the tiny space between them is bridged by chemicals called neurotransmitters. Learn the handover sequence, because reflex-arc questions routinely test the synapse step.

lessons.title: Crossing the synaptic gap
lessons.opening: Neurones never quite touch. Between them sits a synapse — a microscopic gap — and that gap is where chemistry takes over: an arriving impulse makes the first neurone release neurotransmitters, which diffuse across and spark a fresh impulse in the next cell.
keyPoints: Neurones are separated by tiny gaps called synapses.
An arriving electrical impulse triggers neurotransmitter release at the end of a neurone.
Neurotransmitters diffuse over the gap and attach to the next neurone.
Binding generates a new impulse, relaying the message between the separate cells.

low.restatement: Impulse arrives, chemicals cross the gap, next neurone fires — the synapse relays signals between separate cells.
low.analogy: A synapse is a river between islands: the message boards a ferry (the neurotransmitter) to cross.
low.examPointer: Remember both halves: chemical crossing, then a NEW electrical impulse — the impulse itself never jumps.

medium.restatement: Because neurones are not directly connected, transmission needs a chemical bridge: arriving impulses trigger neurotransmitter release, diffusion crosses the gap, and binding regenerates the electrical signal.
medium.analogy: Think of a relay race where the baton is thrown across a short gap rather than handed over.
medium.examPointer: Questions ask what neurotransmitters do — 'diffuse across the synapse and bind' earns the marks; 'travel along the neurone' does not.

options.text: The tiny gap between two neurones
options.explanation: A synapse is the microscopic gap separating neurones.
Neurones are not directly connected — the gap is the point.
Neurotransmitters cross the synapse; they are not it.
That describes a nerve.

check.stem: What triggers the release of neurotransmitters?

options.text: An electrical impulse reaching the end of a neurone
options.explanation: The arriving impulse triggers the chemical release.
Blood flow plays no role in the synapse.
Light is an external stimulus, not the synaptic trigger.

options.text: The next neurone pulling chemicals across
options.explanation: Diffusion carries the chemicals; nothing pulls them.

check.stem: How do neurotransmitters cross the synapse?

options.explanation: Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synapse.

options.text: As electrical impulses jumping the gap
options.explanation: The electrical impulse stops at the gap; chemicals finish the trip.
Molecules do not swim; diffusion does the work.

options.text: Through hollow tubes joining the cells
options.explanation: No tubes connect the neurones.

check.stem: What happens when neurotransmitters bind to the next neurone?

options.text: A new electrical impulse is generated
options.explanation: Binding sparks a fresh impulse in the next cell.

options.text: The next neurone stores them forever
options.explanation: Binding triggers a signal, not storage.
The gap remains open for future transmissions.
The whole point of the relay is to continue the message.

check.stem: Why is a chemical handover needed between two neurones?

options.text: Because the two neurones never actually touch — a gap always separates them
options.explanation: The physical gap forces the chemical relay.
Speed is an advantage, not a problem.

options.text: Because impulses are too large to fit
options.explanation: Impulses have no size in that sense.
Meaningless — molecules do not exercise.

check.stem: Define a synapse and name the chemicals that cross it.
check.modelAnswer: The tiny gap between two neurones, crossed by chemical messengers called neurotransmitters.

check.stem: State the full handover sequence at a synapse.
check.modelAnswer: Impulse arrives, neurotransmitters are released, they diffuse across the synapse, they bind to the next neurone, and a new impulse is generated.

check.stem: Explain why the electrical impulse itself cannot simply continue across the synapse.
check.modelAnswer: The two neurones are separate cells with a real gap between them, so there is no continuous membrane for the electrical signal to travel along; the signal must be converted to chemical form, diffused across, and regenerated as a fresh impulse in the next cell.

check.stem: A poison blocks neurotransmitter release at one synapse in a reflex arc. Predict the effect on the response and justify it.
check.modelAnswer: The response fails: with neurotransmitters blocked, the signal cannot cross that synapse, so no new impulse is generated in the next neurone and the message never reaches the effector — the chain is broken even though every other neurone works.

glossary.definition: The tiny gap between two neurones across which signals are carried chemically.
A chemical messenger released at a synapse that diffuses across and binds to the next neurone, generating a new impulse.
The spreading of molecules from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration, here across the synaptic gap.
